sentences: We want two things that seem to contradict each other: to stay ourselves and to be able to change.
On one hand, we value continuity, being the same person over time, and we are wary of those who "change completely" like a traitor to themselves.
On the other hand, we aspire to evolve, to correct ourselves, to become better, and a life without change would seem like stagnation to us.
How can we reconcile these two demands?
Can we change profoundly while still being ourselves, or does changing necessarily mean ceasing to be who we were?
This question, which concludes our reflection on identity, brings together its threads.
The contradiction is only apparent if we conceive of identity as something fixed, an immutable core that must be preserved intact.
In this view, indeed, changing would be betrayal, altering that essence which should remain the same.
But we have seen that identity may not be a fixed thing, but rather a story, a process, a dynamic continuity.

Now, a story, precisely, is characterized by the fact that it changes while remaining the same story: the narrative of a life incorporates transformations, evolutions, even breaks, without ceasing to be the narrative of a single life.
Change is not the opposite of identity; it is its very movement, provided it is inscribed within a continuity.
For what makes the continuity of an identity through change is not the absence of change, but the way in which changes are linked and integrated.
I remain myself not because I do not change, but because my changes are my own, stemming from my history, connecting to it, even extending it while transforming it.
The child I was, the adult I am, the old person I will be, differ profoundly, and yet a continuity connects them: that of a story that continues, where each stage arises from the previous one.
Changing without betraying oneself means changing within the continuity of one's story, not through arbitrary breaks that would shatter it.
This conception allows us to distinguish two kinds of changes.

There is the change that extends and fulfills, where one becomes more oneself by evolving, where the transformation realizes a continuity rather than breaking it: such is the case for one who matures, deepens, corrects their mistakes while remaining recognizable in what they become.
And there is the change that betrays, where one renounces what they were, where one breaks with their values, where the transformation is a renunciation rather than an accomplishment.
The difference does not lie in the magnitude of the change, but in its relation to continuity: the first is inscribed in a story and continues it, the second breaks it.
Moreover, there are profound changes that, far from betraying, are required by fidelity to oneself.
The one who recognizes their mistake and corrects it, who abandons an untenable conviction, who transforms to remain true to what they hold as true, changes out of fidelity, not betrayal.

True fidelity to oneself is not immobility, the refusal of all change; it is sometimes the ability to change to remain faithful to the essential, to transform what one is in order not to betray what one believes.
Stubbornness in error out of fear of changing would be false fidelity; changing to be more just can be the true fidelity.
Changing without betraying oneself is therefore not only possible but necessary for a vibrant life.
An identity that would refuse all change would freeze, dry up, and cease to be alive; an identity that would change without continuity would dissolve and be lost.

Between stagnation that refuses to evolve and dissolution that loses all thread, there is the path of a living identity: one that changes while remaining faithful to its story, that evolves without renouncing itself, that becomes other while remaining itself.
Ultimately, being oneself does not mean staying identical; it means remaining the coherent author of a story that, to stay alive, never ceases to transform.

sentences: Among the many differences that separate France and Great Britain, the relationship to rules is one of the most revealing, as it touches on deep conceptions of freedom, authority, and social order.
It is often summarized by images: the Briton who queues with discipline, the Frenchman who contests and circumvents.

These images, necessarily simplified, do capture a real difference that deserves to be analyzed beyond the cliché, as it sheds light on two ways of conceiving the link between the individual and the common rule.
The British relationship to rules is based on a fundamental trust.

Rules are generally perceived as legitimate, useful, and an expression of a tacit pact that benefits everyone; respecting them is not submission, but participation in an order that one recognizes as their own.

This trust has historical roots: a political evolution that occurred through progressive reforms rather than breaks, which preserved the continuity of institutions and fostered the feeling that rules emanated from an order to which one adhered.
Respect for rules goes hand in hand with a certain sense of fair play: everyone plays the game because they trust that others will do so as well, and that the game, overall, is fair.
The French relationship to rules is more distrustful, more critical.

Rules are spontaneously suspected, judged, and required to justify themselves; they are not respected by principle, but to the extent that they are recognized as founded, and one reserves the right to contest, circumvent, or even oppose them if deemed unjust.

This disposition also has historical roots: a political history made up of breaks and revolutions, where contesting established authority has been elevated to a founding virtue; a tradition that sees critical spirit and resistance to arbitrariness as cardinal values.
Contesting the rule is not seen as incivility, but often as an affirmation of one's freedom and judgment.
These two relationships stem from two conceptions of freedom.

For the British sensibility, freedom accommodates the respect for rules, provided they are just and accepted; obeying a rule that one recognizes as legitimate does not alienate in any way, and order is the condition for everyone's freedom.

For the French sensibility, freedom implies the permanent right to judge the rule, not to submit to it blindly, and to resist what one deems unjust; obedience without examination seems suspect, as an abdication of judgment.
One sees in the rule a pact that protects freedom; the other sees a power that must be treated with caution.
Each of these relationships has its virtues and vices, and one illuminates the other by contrast.

The British respect for rules produces an orderly, fluid, courteous society, where communal life unfolds with remarkable civility; but it can lead to a docility that accepts rules that deserve to be contested, and a conformism that confuses order with justice.

The French critical spirit maintains a salutary vigilance against arbitrariness, a capacity to resist injustice; but it can degenerate into chronic indiscipline, systematic contestation, and difficulty in agreeing on common rules and enforcing them.
Understanding these two relationships means understanding that neither holds the truth, but that each reveals the limits of the other.
The Briton would sometimes benefit from contesting more, the Frenchman from respecting more; one could learn from the other's critical vigilance, the other from their civic trust.
Neither disposition is superior in itself: they respond differently to the same tension between the order that makes communal life possible and the freedom that refuses to submit to it blindly.

Observing them in relation to each other allows us to realize that our own relationship to rules, which we believe to be natural, is actually a choice among other possibilities — and to discover, in the neighbor's mirror, what our own assumptions have of particular.

sentences: Abundance societies have realized a millennia-old dream of humanity: they have largely conquered scarcity, providing their members with a profusion of goods, leisure, and opportunities that past generations would not have dared to dream of.
One might expect this abundance to bring happiness in proportion to it.
However, a paradox emerges: within this very profusion, a feeling of emptiness, dissatisfaction, and sometimes depression spreads.
Why is it that abundance, far from filling, often seems to deepen a void?
This question strikes at the heart of the malaise in wealthy societies.
A first explanation lies in the mechanism of habituation and desire.
We quickly get used to what we possess; the long-desired good, once obtained, rapidly ceases to bring us joy, and a new desire takes its place.
Abundance, by satisfying our desires, does not therefore soothe desire itself, which shifts and renews endlessly.
We get what we want, and immediately we want something else; satisfaction is brief, and lack is perpetual.
Abundance does not fill desire; it sustains it, keeping us in a state of dissatisfaction that no good can satisfy.
The more we have, the more we want, and the void deepens as our possessions increase.
A second explanation relates to the nature of what abundance provides.
It offers us material goods, pleasures, and entertainment; but these things do not fulfill the deepest need of human beings, which is a need for meaning, relationships, and fulfillment.
Material abundance can coexist with a poverty of meaning; one can have everything that can be bought and lack what cannot be purchased.

The emptiness within abundance may be that of a need that abundance cannot fulfill, because it pertains to something else: it fills our lives with goods, but not with meaning, and it is meaning that we hunger for.
There is something more troubling.
Abundance itself can generate a particular form of emptiness, due to the excess of choices it offers.
Faced with a profusion of possibilities, we are paralyzed, unable to choose, dissatisfied with our choices that deprive us of all others, haunted by what we could have had.
The abundance of possibilities, far from liberating, can overwhelm; too many choices lead to indecision, regret, and dissatisfaction.
We have so many options that we no longer know how to want them, so many possibilities that we do not fully realize any of them, scattered in a field of possibilities where we fixate on nothing.
The abundance of possibilities is also a dispersion, where emptiness arises from excess.
This diagnosis does not lead to praising scarcity, nor to regretting material poverty, which has been and remains a very real misfortune.
The emptiness of abundance is a problem of the rich, and it would be indecent to compare it to the distress of lack.

But it reveals an important truth: that the satisfaction of material needs, however necessary it may be, is not enough for happiness, and that a civilization that has conquered scarcity without addressing the need for meaning would not have conquered unhappiness.
Abundance solves one problem — that of material lack — without resolving the one that persists beyond: the need for meaning, relationships, and fulfillment, which no profusion of goods can satisfy.
Thus, escaping the emptiness of abundance does not mean renouncing it, but understanding what it cannot give, and seeking it elsewhere.

It is to recognize that meaning cannot be bought, that deep relationships cannot be consumed, that fulfillment is not found in possession; it is to stop expecting from material abundance what it cannot provide, in order to invest in what alone fulfills the deepest need.
It may also be about learning to desire differently, to step out of the race for possession that sustains lack, to find in sufficiency what excess does not provide.

The emptiness of abundance is not a fatality; it is a sign that we are looking in the wrong place for what abundance does not contain — and that we must, even within the profusion, relearn where to find what truly fulfills.

sentences: The phrase 'Beauty will save the world' comes from a great novelist, as famous as he is enigmatic, and it keeps resurfacing, fervently quoted, even though we don't always know what it means.
How could beauty, which seems so powerless and so foreign to the forces that govern the world, save it?
What would it save it from, and by what power?
At first glance, the phrase seems like a beautiful empty word, a pious wish of an aesthete.
But perhaps it holds a deep intuition worth exploring about the power of beauty and what our world needs saving from.
First, we must clear up misunderstandings.

The phrase obviously does not mean that contemplating beautiful things would solve the world's problems, that art could replace political or moral action, or that beauty would be a solution to concrete miseries.
Such an interpretation would be naive, and even indecent: beauty has never fed the hungry nor stopped tyrants.
If the phrase has any meaning, it is not one of beauty's practical effectiveness, which it has none.
It is elsewhere that we must look for what beauty could 'save', in a realm that is not about action, but about what underpins or precedes it.

Perhaps beauty saves in that it testifies, against the evil and ugliness of the world, that something else is possible, that there exists a value, an order, a harmony that cannot be reduced to chaos, violence, or self-interest.
In a world marked by moral and physical ugliness, beauty is like a promise, a sign that evil does not have the last word, that there is something worthwhile, something that elevates and transcends.

It does not fight evil directly, but it preserves from despair those who, without it, might believe that everything is just ugliness; it keeps alive the idea that there is a value, without which the struggle against evil would lose its meaning.
Beauty perhaps saves in that it keeps open the dimension of value, without which there would be nothing to save.
There is more.
Beauty could save in that it transforms the one who contemplates it, opening them to something beyond their own interest, pulling them out of self-absorption.

The experience of beauty is disinterested: in the presence of what is beautiful, we do not seek to possess, to use, or to benefit; we contemplate, we forget ourselves, we open ourselves to what transcends us.
This experience educates us to a relationship with the world that is not one of greed, possession, or utility; it teaches us to value what is useless, to respect what is valuable for itself.
In this sense, beauty could 'save' by forming within us a disposition — disinterestedness, contemplation, respect for what transcends our interest — that the world, precisely, sorely lacks.
But we must be careful not to idealize beauty, as if it were always on the side of good.

For beauty can also seduce, deceive, and serve evil; there are moral uglinesses that adorn themselves in beauty, criminal powers that have cultivated superb art, aesthetic seductions employed for the worst.
Beauty is not necessarily moral; it can enchant, divert, and make one accept the unacceptable under beautiful appearances.
To believe that beauty would always save, that it would inherently be on the side of good, would be a dangerous naivety, contradicted by history.
Beauty is ambivalent, like any power; it can elevate or seduce, open to good or divert from it.
What can we conclude from this meditation?
Perhaps the phrase, rather than being an assertion, is a question or a fragile hope.
Beauty will not automatically save the world, nor by an effectiveness it does not possess, nor because it is always on the side of good.
But it can, if we know how to welcome it, preserve within us the dimension of value, open us to disinterestedness, and testify that something else is possible beyond ugliness and evil.

In this precise and limited sense, it participates in what could save the world — not alone, not by magic, but as one of the signs and one of the forces that keep alive the idea that there is something worthwhile, and that deserves to be saved.
Beauty does not save the world; but a world that has lost even the sense of beauty would undoubtedly already be lost.
Perhaps this is what the phrase means: not that beauty is enough, but that without it, nothing would suffice.

alignments.french: La beauté n'est pas nécessairement morale ; elle peut envoûter, détourner, faire accepter l'inacceptable sous de belles apparences.
alignments.english: Beauty is not necessarily moral; it can enchant, divert, and make one accept the unacceptable under beautiful appearances.

alignments.french: Croire que la beauté sauverait toujours, qu'elle serait par nature du côté du bien, serait une naïveté dangereuse, que dément l'histoire.
alignments.english: To believe that beauty would always save, that it would inherently be on the side of good, would be a dangerous naivety, contradicted by history.

alignments.french: La beauté est ambivalente, comme toute puissance ; elle peut élever ou séduire, ouvrir au bien ou en détourner.
alignments.english: Beauty is ambivalent, like any power; it can elevate or seduce, open to good or divert from it.
What can we conclude from this meditation?

alignments.french: Peut-être que la formule, plutôt qu'une affirmation, est une question, ou une espérance fragile.
alignments.english: Perhaps the phrase, rather than being an assertion, is a question or a fragile hope.

alignments.french: La beauté ne sauvera pas le monde automatiquement, ni par une efficacité qu'elle n'a pas, ni parce qu'elle serait toujours du côté du bien.
alignments.english: Beauty will not automatically save the world, nor by an effectiveness it does not possess, nor because it is always on the side of good.

alignments.french: Mais elle peut, si nous savons l'accueillir, préserver en nous la dimension de la valeur, nous ouvrir au désintéressement, témoigner qu'autre chose est possible que la laideur et le mal.
alignments.english: But it can, if we know how to welcome it, preserve within us the dimension of value, open us to disinterestedness, and testify that something else is possible beyond ugliness and evil.

alignments.french: En ce sens précis et limité, elle participe à ce qui pourrait sauver le monde — non seule, non par magie, mais comme l'un des signes et l'une des forces qui maintiennent vivante l'idée qu'il existe quelque chose qui vaut, et qui mérite qu'on le sauve.
alignments.english: In this precise and limited sense, it participates in what could save the world — not alone, not by magic, but as one of the signs and one of the forces that keep alive the idea that there is something worthwhile, and that deserves to be saved.

alignments.french: La beauté ne sauve pas le monde ; mais un monde qui aurait perdu jusqu'au sens de la beauté serait sans doute déjà perdu.
alignments.english: Beauty does not save the world; but a world that has lost even the sense of beauty would undoubtedly already be lost.

alignments.french: C'est peut-être cela que dit la formule : non que la beauté suffise, mais que sans elle, rien ne suffirait.
alignments.english: Perhaps this is what the phrase means: not that beauty is enough, but that without it, nothing would suffice.

sentences: Every morning, around ten o'clock, the postman comes down my street.
His name is Marc.
He has a yellow bike and a big bag of letters.
Marc knows everyone.
He knows the names, the houses, the dogs.
He says hello to everyone, even when it rains.
"The postman is the neighborhood's newspaper," says my grandmother.
That's true.
Marc knows everything: the new baby, the new neighbors, the lost and found cat.
As for me, I mostly receive advertisements.
Pizzas, supermarkets.
Sometimes, a bill.
I throw away almost everything.
But this morning, it's different.
Marc rings my doorbell.
"A letter for you!
A real one!" he says, happy.
A real letter, with a stamp.
I recognize the handwriting: it's my cousin Emma, in Canada.
I open the letter with a coffee.
Emma talks about her new life, her job, the snow.
She writes: "Write back to me with a real letter."
This afternoon, I buy some paper and a stamp.
A real letter feels good.
Thank you, Emma.
And thank you, Marc.

sentences: At the end of these reflections on time, memory, and identity, one question remains, the most existential of all: how do we live with the passage of time?

For everything we have said comes down to this observation: time passes, taking everything with it—our days, our joys, our loved ones, ourselves; and this passage is the source of our deepest anxieties.
In the face of it, two opposing temptations arise, both equally futile; and perhaps there is a third way, more difficult but wiser, where a form of peace could be found.
The first temptation is to want to hold on to what passes, to fight against the passage of time, to try to stop the moment, to preserve what is leaving.
This temptation is deeply human: we would like to freeze the happy moment, keep what we love, prevent time from tearing away what is dear to us.
But this struggle is doomed from the start, and wanting to hold on to what passes is to condemn oneself to the suffering of perpetual failure.
We cannot hold back time; it slips away regardless of what we do, and clinging to what is leaving, refusing its passage, only adds the pain of futile resistance to the inevitable loss.

He who wants to hold on to the moment misses it, for he does not live it, so preoccupied is he with wanting to fix it; and he suffers doubly, from the passage he cannot prevent and from his own powerlessness.
The second, opposite temptation is to resign oneself to the passage of time, to detach oneself from it, to give up on attaching to what will pass anyway.
Since everything goes away, why bother to attach?
It would be better not to love too much, not to hold anything as precious, to protect oneself against loss by refusing attachment.
This wisdom of detachment, advocated by certain traditions, has its nobility and coherence; but it also has its price, which is to deprive oneself of life itself.
For not attaching to anything to avoid losing anything is to renounce love, enjoyment, and living fully; it is to protect oneself from the pain of loss at the cost of the richness of attachment.
Total detachment avoids suffering, but it also avoids life; it buys peace at the price of emptiness.
Between these two temptations—holding on to what passes or detaching from it—there may be a third way, more difficult, where a form of wisdom could be found.

It would consist of loving what passes not despite its passage, but in a sense because of it; savoring the moment precisely because it is unique and will not return; cherishing what is dear to us knowing that we will lose it, and loving all the more intensely because we know the loss is inevitable.

This way does not deny the passage of time, as the first temptation does; it does not protect itself from it through detachment, as the second does; it accepts it, and makes it the very source of the value of what passes.
For it is because the moment flees that it is precious; it is because we die that life has value; it is because nothing lasts that everything deserves to be fully lived.
This wisdom is difficult, for it requires holding together what seems contradictory: attachment and consent to loss, love of what passes and acceptance of its flight.

It does not eliminate the pain of losing—this pain is the price of attachment, and refusing it would be to refuse to love—but it transforms our relationship to loss, making finitude not the enemy of value, but its condition.

Loving a being knowing that we will lose it, savoring a moment knowing that it is fleeting, is not to condemn oneself to suffering; it is to love and savor fully, with that intensity that only the awareness of finitude can provide.
The passing time, in this perspective, is no longer just what tears away what we love; it is what gives what we love its irreplaceable value.
Holding on to what passes is impossible; detaching from it is impoverishing; what remains is to love it because it passes.

This is perhaps the highest wisdom regarding time: not the futile struggle against its passage, nor the detachment that deprives us of life, but a lucid and loving consent to finitude, which makes the passage of time not a curse, but the very source of the value and beauty of what is given to us.
Time takes everything from us; but it is also what, by making everything ephemeral, makes everything precious.

Consenting to this, loving fully what we know we must lose, living each moment as unique because it is, is perhaps the only possible victory over time: not to stop it, which is impossible, but to inhabit it so fully that its very passage becomes a reason to love.

sentences: The end justifies the means." This phrase, often quoted to be condemned, expresses one of the most troubling issues in the morality of action: can one do evil for the sake of a greater good?
Is it permissible to resort to condemnable means if the goal pursued is good, or even necessary?
This question is not academic; it arises in real action, especially in politics, where it is often claimed that one must do evil for a greater good.
Answering it requires untangling what the phrase mixes, and resisting two overly simple responses.
The first simple response is the one that unreservedly approves the phrase: yes, the end justifies the means, and if the goal is good, any means to achieve it is legitimate.
This position, often attributed to those in power, has an appearance of realism: in action, it says, one cannot afford scruples, one must be effective, and only the result matters.

But taken to its extreme, this position is monstrous: it justifies all crimes in the name of the ends they would serve, it abolishes any moral limit, and it makes the goal a universal justification for any means.

If the end really justified all means, then the worst atrocities would be permitted in the name of supposedly good goals, and history shows where this logic leads: to crimes committed in the name of brighter tomorrows, to horrors justified by the ends they were supposed to serve.

The second simple, opposite response absolutely condemns the phrase: no, the end never justifies the means, and certain acts are forbidden regardless of their consequences, no matter what good they might produce.
This position, more noble, asserts that there are limits that nothing can lift, acts that no end could justify, a dignity of the person that cannot be sacrificed for any goal.
It has on its side moral firmness, the refusal of the slope that justifies everything by the ends.

But it also encounters a difficulty: for there seem to be cases where absolutely refusing any condemnable means would lead to worse consequences, where intransigence on means would sacrifice immense goods.
Should we allow innocents to perish rather than transgress a rule?
The absolutism of means can also lead to results that are hard to accept.

Between these two positions, moral reflection has sought more nuanced paths, which recognize the complexity of the problem without yielding to either the cynicism that justifies everything or an absolutism that ignores the consequences.

One can distinguish according to the means: some are so radically contrary to dignity — torture, the murder of innocents — that no end could justify them, while others, lesser ones, can be weighed against the ends.
One can distinguish according to the ends: not all are equal, and the invoked good must be real, certain, proportional, not a distant and hypothetical pretext.

One can recognize that action sometimes involves the tragic, those situations where every choice is culpable, where one cannot act without getting their hands dirty, and where one must assume the share of evil in their action without absolving themselves.
For perhaps this is where the deepest truth about this question lies: in the recognition of the tragic nature of action.

The one who acts, especially in public affairs, is sometimes confronted with situations where every option involves evil, where one must choose the lesser evil without that lesser evil ceasing to be evil.

Lucidity then consists not in persuading oneself that the end justifies the means, erasing the fault, nor in refusing to act in the name of purity, but in assuming the share of evil in one's action while recognizing it as such.

The responsible person of action is neither the cynic who believes themselves justified by their ends, nor the pure who refuses to get their hands dirty; it is the one who, sometimes forced into dubious means, bears the weight of it without absolving themselves, who retains a sense of fault even when they believe they must commit it.
The phrase 'the end justifies the means' is therefore both false and incomplete.
False, if it means that the goal erases the nature of the means, that anything is permitted in the name of the ends; that would abolish all morality.
Incomplete, because it ignores the complexity: that some means are absolutely forbidden, that others can be weighed, that action sometimes involves the tragic.

True wisdom is neither to justify everything by the ends, nor to ignore the consequences in the name of abstract purity, but to hold together the respect for absolute limits, the weighing of consequences, and the tragic lucidity that assumes the share of evil in action without ever absolving itself.
The end does not justify the means; but it does not make them indifferent either; and acting morally, in an imperfect world, often means bearing the weight of this tearing.

sentences: Technical progress has given humanity unprecedented powers: we can transform nature, extend life, communicate instantly across the world, and also destroy on a scale once unimaginable.
These powers are constantly growing, and nothing seems to be able to limit them.
But a question arises, all the more pressing as these powers increase: does our wisdom keep pace with our powers?
Have we become, as our power has grown, wiser and more capable of using what we can do wisely?
And if that is not the case, if our powers are growing faster than our wisdom, what do we risk?
The observation is hard to refute: our technical powers have grown tremendously, but nothing indicates that our wisdom has progressed proportionately.
We are not evidently wiser, fairer, or more in control of our passions than people of the past; we have infinitely more powerful means, but we use them for purposes that are no wiser.
This is a formidable imbalance: for increased power in hands that are not wiser is more dangerous, not less, than lesser power.
The more powerful our means are, the graver our faults can be, and the more catastrophic the consequences of our lack of wisdom can be.
The imbalance between our powers and our wisdom may be the major peril of our time.
This imbalance is strikingly evident in our capacity for destruction.
Humanity has, for the first time in its history, acquired the power to destroy itself, to make the planet uninhabitable, to annihilate civilization.
This terrifying power is in the hands of a humanity that is no wiser than before, still subject to the same passions, the same blind spots, the same follies.
The fact that this unparalleled power of destruction is held by a humanity whose wisdom has not grown proportionately should fill us with concern.
We have the means to destroy ourselves, without having acquired the wisdom that would surely protect us from it.
This imbalance is also evident in our relationship with nature.

Our technical powers have given us an unprecedented ability to transform our environment, but we use it without the wisdom that would measure the consequences, preserve the balances, and safeguard the future.
We are transforming the world on a scale that exceeds our ability to foresee and control the effects, with a power that surpasses our wisdom.

The result is the ecological crisis, which may be the most visible manifestation of the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom: we can transform the planet, but we are not wise enough to do so without destroying it.
Should we conclude that we need to limit technological progress, renouncing powers that our wisdom cannot control?
This conclusion, appealing as it is, is difficult to implement, because no one can stop technological progress, and wanting to do so would be futile.
The real answer may lie elsewhere: not in the illusory limitation of powers, but in the development of wisdom, so that it catches up with our powers.
If our powers grow faster than our wisdom, the solution is not to restrain the powers, but to increase wisdom, ensuring that it grows in proportion to our strength.

This is an immense challenge, as wisdom does not progress like technology, does not accumulate, and must be reclaimed by each generation; but it is the only one that can address the imbalance that threatens us.
This challenge gives a new meaning to what we have said about wisdom, virtue, and self-formation.
For if the major peril of our time is the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom, then the development of wisdom—both individual and collective—is not a luxury, but a vital necessity.

Cultivating wisdom, prudence, self-control, a sense of limits, and responsibility towards the future is not just a matter of personal improvement; it may be the very condition for the survival of humanity, whose powers have exceeded control.

Technological progress, without progress in wisdom, leads to catastrophe; and the great challenge of our time may be to ensure that our wisdom finally catches up with our powers, before the imbalance becomes fatal.
Never has the ancient demand for wisdom been as urgent as in an age where our powers have become excessive.

sentences: Death concerns us not only as our own, to come; it also affects us, and perhaps more painfully, as that of the beings we love.
Losing a loved one is one of the hardest trials of existence, and the question of how to live after this loss, how to go through grief, is one of the most difficult there is.
For grief places us before an apparent dilemma: between forgetting, which seems to betray the one we've lost, and perpetual pain, which freezes us in the loss and prevents us from living.
How can we be faithful to the one we've lost without allowing grief to destroy us?
Grief is primarily a pain, and it would be indecent to want to eliminate it, to pretend to free oneself from it too quickly.
The loss of a loved one is a real tearing; the pain of grief is legitimate, even necessary, as it measures the love we had.
Wanting to escape grief too quickly, rushing to 'turn the page,' would be a way of betraying the one we've lost, denying the importance they had.
Grief requires its time, its work, its pain; we must not rush it, nor be ashamed to suffer, nor let ourselves be pressured to heal.
The pain of grief is the first tribute to the one we've lost.
But grief cannot also be frozen in perpetual pain, in a sorrow that would trap us forever in loss.

Staying indefinitely in pain, refusing to live after the loss, allowing oneself to be destroyed by sorrow, is not honoring the one we lost either; it is letting oneself die with them, refusing the life they would have wanted for us.
There comes a moment when grief, if it does not transform, becomes a prison, a misunderstood fidelity that freezes us in death instead of returning us to life.
Remaining forever in pain is no more faithful than forgetting; it is another way of failing to honor what we owe to the one we lost, and to the life that continues.
How can we escape this dilemma between the betrayal of forgetting and the paralysis of pain?
Perhaps by understanding that true fidelity to the deceased is neither forgetting nor perpetual pain, but the transformation of the bond.

The work of mourning is not to forget the one we lost, nor to remain frozen in sorrow, but to transform our relationship with them: from a lost presence, whose absence tears us apart, to an inner presence, a living memory that accompanies us.
The one we lost does not completely disappear; they remain within us, in what they gave us, in what we learned from them, in the way they continue to inspire us.
Fidelity to the deceased means keeping them alive within us, not as a wound that never heals, but as a presence that nourishes, accompanies, and inspires.
This transformation of the bond allows us to reconcile fidelity and life.
For keeping alive within us the one we have lost, making their memory live on, allowing their influence to continue to guide us, is not to forget them; it is to remain faithful to them.
And this fidelity, far from freezing us in pain, brings us back to life, as it transforms loss into legacy, absence into inner presence, and sorrow into living memory.
We can live after loss, regain joy, look towards the future, all while remaining faithful to the one we have lost, by keeping them alive within us.
True fidelity is not about refusing to live, but about living while carrying within us the one we have lost, making fruitful what they have given us.
Grief, understood this way, is not a choice between forgetting and pain, but a work of transformation, which moves from lost presence to inner presence, from heartbreaking absence to living memory.
This work is long, painful, never quite finished; but it allows us to reconcile fidelity to the deceased and a return to life, to honor the one we have lost without being destroyed by their absence.

And it reveals a truth about love and death: that death separates, but does not entirely destroy the bond; that those we have loved continue to live within us, in what they have given us; and that fidelity to the dead is not about dying with them, but about keeping them alive within us while we ourselves live.

Loving those who are no longer here means carrying them within us, not as a weight that crushes, but as a presence that accompanies — and this may be the highest way to conquer, if not death, at least its power to destroy what love once was.

sentences: Everything having been agreed upon, from this day forward, the preparations for the perilous expedition were carried out quickly.
The men had bravely accepted the fact that they had six hundred miles to cover under these conditions.
Sergeant Long was in charge of the work, while Jasper Hobson, the two hunters, and Mrs.
Paulina Barnett frequently went to assess the state of the icefield.
Kalumah accompanied them most often, and his advice, based on experience, could be very useful to the lieutenant.
The departure, barring any unforeseen circumstances, was set for November 20, so there was no time to lose.
As Jasper Hobson had predicted, with the wind picking up, the temperature dropped a bit, and the mercury column registered twenty-four degrees Fahrenheit (4°, 44 degrees Celsius below zero).
The snow replaced the rain from the previous days and was hardening on the ground.
A few days of this cold, and the sliding of the sleds would become possible.
The notch, dug in front of Cape Michel, was partly filled with ice and snow, but it should not be forgotten that its calmer waters must have frozen more quickly.
What proved this well was that the waters of the sea did not present as satisfactory a state.
Ce qui le prouvait bien, c'est que les eaux de la mer ne présentaient pas un état aussi satisfaisant.
Madam, replied the captain, whatever a man can do, Jasper Hobson will do it.
The Company has tasked him with exploring the north of its territories and establishing a trading post as close as possible to the limits of the American continent, and he will establish it.
--That's a great responsibility that falls on Lieutenant Hobson!
said the traveler.
--Yes, madam, but Jasper Hobson has never shied away from a task to be accomplished, no matter how tough it might be.
--I believe you, captain, replied Mrs.
Paulina, and we will see this lieutenant in action.
But what interest drives the Company to build a fort at the edge of the Arctic Sea?
--That would indeed be, replied Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, a significant result if the Northwest Passage can be used.
But you mentioned a double interest, I believe?
The other point, madam, the captain continued, here it is, and it is, so to speak, a vital issue for the Company, of which I will ask your permission to remind you of its origin in a few words.

You will then understand why this association, once so prosperous, is now threatened at the very source of its products." In a few words, indeed, Captain Craventy provided the history of this famous Company.

Sir, you have pronounced this word twice now?

sentences: Nothing seemed changed to me.
The castle still soaked its grayish walls in the pond at the entrance of the small town; and the inn was the same, although repaired, renovated, with a more modern look.
Upon entering, I was greeted by two young Breton women of eighteen, fresh and kind, clad in their tight wool vests, wearing silver caps with large embroidered plaques on their ears.
It was around six o'clock in the evening.
I sat down to dinner and, as the owner himself hurried to serve me, fate perhaps made me say: 'Did you know the former owners of this house?
I spent about ten days here thirty years ago now.
I'm speaking to you from afar.' Then I told him the occasion for which I had stopped, how I had been held back by a friend's illness.
He didn't let me finish.
'Oh!
I remember perfectly. I was then fifteen or sixteen.
You were sleeping in the back room and your friend in the one I made mine, on the street.' It was only then that the very vivid memory of the little maid came back to me.
I asked: 'Do you remember a nice little servant your father had then, who had, if my memory serves me right, pretty blue eyes and fresh teeth?'

sentences: Indeed, Mr. Hobson, the traveler replied, is there a mode of transportation more pleasant than ours?
We don't feel like we're moving.
Our island has precisely the same speed as that of the current that carries it away.
Isn't it the same phenomenon that accompanies a balloon in the air?
And what a charm it would be to travel like this with your house, your garden, your park, your very country!
A wandering island, but I mean a real island, with a solid, unsinkable base, would truly be the most comfortable and wonderful vehicle one could imagine.
They say hanging gardens have been made?
Why, one day, wouldn't we create floating parks that would transport us to all corners of the world?
Their size would make them completely insensitive to the waves.
They would have nothing to fear from storms.
Perhaps even, with favorable winds, we could steer them with large sails stretched to the breeze?
And then, what miraculous vegetation would surprise the eyes of the passengers when they passed from temperate zones to tropical zones!
I even imagine that with skilled pilots, well-trained in the currents, we could maintain ourselves under chosen latitudes and enjoy an eternal spring at will!

sentences: Selim, still holding his burning wick in his hand, came to the opening, bowed radiantly under the beam of light, and picked up the sign.
The messenger let out a cry of joy and clapped his hands.
At this signal, four soldiers of the seraskier Kourchid rushed in, and Selim fell, pierced by five dagger blows.
Each had delivered his own.
And yet, drunk with their crime, though still pale with fear, they rushed into the underground, searching everywhere for fire and rolling on the bags of gold.
Meanwhile, my mother seized me in her arms, and, agile, bounding through the twists known only to us, she reached a hidden staircase of the kiosk where a terrifying tumult reigned.
The lower halls were completely filled with Kourchid's Tchodoars, that is to say, our enemies.
Just as my mother was about to push the small door, we heard the terrible and threatening voice of the pasha resound.
My mother pressed her eye to the cracks in the boards; an opening happened to be right in front of mine, and I looked.
--What do you want?
my father said to some people holding a paper with golden characters in their hands.

sentences: I have never lost hope, Mr. Hobson, replied the traveler.
Men like your companions and you would not be defeated by the hardships of a winter!

Madam, since I have been living in the polar regions, replied Lieutenant Hobson, I have never experienced such cold, and to be honest, if it had persisted a few more days, I believe we would have truly been lost.
So this earthquake came just in time to drive away those cursed bears, said the traveler, and perhaps it contributed to changing this extreme temperature?
That is possible, madam, very possible indeed, replied the lieutenant.
All these natural phenomena are connected and influence each other.
But, I must admit, the volcanic composition of this soil worries me.
I regret, for our settlement, the proximity of this active volcano.
If its lava cannot reach it, it at least causes tremors that jeopardize it!
Look at what our house looks like now!
You will have it repaired, Mr. Hobson, as soon as the nice season arrives, replied Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, and you will take advantage of the experience to reinforce it more solidly.
Certainly, madam, but as it is now and for a few more months, I'm afraid it may not seem comfortable enough for you!

sentences: The notary locked the door and began the reading after unsealing the red wax envelope in front of us, unaware of its contents.
Suddenly, my friend fell silent, stood up, then went to take an old paper from his desk, unfolded it, kissed it longingly, and continued.

Here is the will of my beloved mother: "I, the undersigned Anne-Catherine-Geneviève-Mathilde de Croixluce, legitimate wife of Jean-Léopold-Joseph Gontran de Courcils, sound in body and mind, express here my last wishes.
I ask for forgiveness from God first, and then from my dear son René, for the act I am about to commit.
I believe my child is big enough in heart to understand and forgive me.
I have suffered all my life.
I was married for convenience, then despised, unrecognized, oppressed, and constantly deceived by my husband.
My older sons did not love me, did not spoil me, and treated me barely as a mother.
I was for them, during my life, what I was supposed to be; I owe them nothing after my death.
The ties of blood do not exist without the constant, sacred affection of each day.
An ungrateful son is less than a stranger; he is a guilty one, for he has no right to be indifferent to his mother.

sentences: Caderousse entered eagerly and was the first.
Then, seeing the downstairs room empty as usual and simply watched over by his dog, he called for his wife.
"Hey!"
Carconte, he said, that worthy priest didn't deceive us; the diamond is genuine.
A joyful exclamation was heard, and almost immediately the staircase creaked under a step weighed down by weakness and illness.
"I say the diamond is genuine; here is a gentleman, one of the top jewelers in Paris, who is ready to give us fifty thousand francs for it.
However, to be sure that the diamond truly belongs to us, he asks that you tell him, as I have already done, how the diamond miraculously came into our hands.
In the meantime, sir, please have a seat, and since the weather is heavy, I will go get something to refresh you.
The jeweler was carefully examining the interior of the inn and the visible poverty of those who were about to sell him a diamond that seemed to come from a prince's jewel box.
"Tell me, madam," he said, wanting no doubt to take advantage of the husband's absence so that no sign from him would influence the woman, and to see if the two stories would match up well.
"But how did he come to possess this diamond?"
the jeweler asked.
Did he have it before going to prison?

"No, sir," the woman replied, "but in prison he apparently made the acquaintance of a very wealthy Englishman; and since his cellmate fell ill, and Dantès took care of him as if he were his brother, the Englishman, upon leaving captivity, left the poor Dantès, who, less fortunate than him, died in prison, this diamond which he bequeathed to us in turn upon his death, and which he asked the worthy abbé who came this morning to deliver to us.

sentences: Morrel understood that the old man placed great importance on this oath.
"On my honor," he said, "I swear to wait for what you decide in order to act against Mr.
d'Épinay.
"Now," Morrel continued, "may I, sir, have your son kiss you just as your daughter did a moment ago!" There was no mistaking the expression in Noirtier's eyes.
The young man pressed his lips to the old man's forehead in the same spot where the young girl had placed hers.
In the courtyard, he found the old servant, informed by Valentine; he was waiting for Morrel and guided him through the twists of a dark corridor that led to a small door opening onto the garden.

Once there, Morrel reached the gate, and by the arbor, he was at the top of the wall in an instant, and with his ladder, he was in the alfalfa enclosure in a second, where his cabriolet was always waiting for him.

He got back in, and overwhelmed by so many emotions, but with a lighter heart, he returned around midnight to rue Meslay, threw himself onto his bed, and slept as if he had been plunged into a deep intoxication.
Two days later, a considerable crowd had gathered around ten in the morning at Mr.
de Villefort's door, and a long line of funeral carriages and private vehicles had been seen advancing all along the faubourg Saint-Honoré and rue de la Pépinière.
Among these vehicles, there was one of a peculiar shape that seemed to have made a long journey.
It was a kind of black-painted van that had been one of the first to arrive at the funeral meeting.

sentences: You are right, madam, replied Jasper Hobson.
You understand these matters perfectly, and I have nothing to say in response to your observation,
unless, of course, there exists some unknown current that is not yet marked on this map.
Indeed, this uncertainty is dreadful.
I wish it were tomorrow so that I could be definitively settled on the situation of the island.
So there was nothing left to do but wait.
They parted ways.
Everyone returned to their usual activities.
Sergeant Long informed his companions that the departure for Fort Reliance, scheduled for the next day, would not take place.

He explained that, after further consideration, the season was too advanced to reach the trading post before the severe cold, that the astronomer had decided to endure another wintering to complete his meteorological observations, and that the resupply of Fort Esperance was not essential, etc.
These were all things that these brave people cared little about.

Lieutenant Hobson made a special recommendation to the hunters, advising them to spare the fur-bearing animals from now on, which he had no use for, and to focus on edible game in order to replenish the factory's supplies.

He also forbade them from straying more than two miles from the fort, not wanting Marbre, Sabine, or other hunters to unexpectedly find themselves facing a horizon of sea, where a few months ago, the isthmus connecting Victoria Peninsula to the American continent had developed.
The disappearance of this narrow strip of land would indeed have revealed the situation.
This day seemed endless to Lieutenant Hobson.
He returned several times to the summit of Cape Bathurst, either alone or accompanied by Mrs.
Paulina Barnett.
The traveler, a woman of strong spirit, was not at all frightened.
The future did not seem daunting to her.
She even joked with Jasper Hobson, saying that this drifting island they were on might be the true vehicle to reach the North Pole!
With a favorable current, why wouldn't they reach this inaccessible point on the globe?

sentences: I was about to take my usual place on the raft when my uncle stopped me with his hand.

"I mustn't overlook anything," he replied, "and since fate has brought me to this part of the coast, I won't leave without having explored it." This remark will be understood when one knows that we had returned to the northern shore, but not to the exact spot of our original departure.
Port-Graüben was supposed to be located further west.
It was therefore only reasonable to carefully examine the surroundings of this new landing.
And, leaving Hans to his tasks, we set off.
The space between the sea's edge and the foot of the foothills was quite wide; one could walk for half an hour before reaching the rock face.
Our feet crushed countless shells of all shapes and sizes, where the animals of the earliest epochs lived.
I also spotted enormous shells, whose diameter often exceeded fifteen feet.
They belonged to those gigantic glyptodonts from the Pliocene period, of which modern turtles are merely a small remnant.
Moreover, the ground was strewn with a large quantity of rocky debris, rounded pebbles shaped by the waves and arranged in successive lines.
I was thus led to make this observation, that the sea must have once occupied this space.
On the scattered rocks, now out of its reach, the waves had left clear traces of their passage.
This could explain to some extent the existence of this ocean, forty leagues below the surface of the globe.
But, in my view, this body of water must gradually be lost in the depths of the earth, and it obviously originated from the waters of the Ocean, which broke through some fissure.
However, it had to be acknowledged that this fissure was currently blocked, for this entire cavern, or rather this immense reservoir, would have filled up in a relatively short time.
Perhaps even this water, having had to battle against underground fires, had partially vaporized.
Hence the explanation for the clouds hanging above our heads and the release of this electricity that created storms within the earth's mass.

sentences: Immediately, Engineer Serkö and Captain Spade move closer to him, and fearing that he might fall into the sea, they hold him firmly and then bring him back onto the deck.
I also observe,
--for I have long experience,
--that Thomas Roch is in the grip of intense agitation.
He spins around, he gestures, incoherent phrases that are directed at no one come out of his mouth...
This is all too evident; a crisis is imminent,
He is experiencing a crisis similar to the one that seized him during his last evening at Healthful-House, the consequences of which were so dire.
We will have to take hold of him and bring him down to his cabin, where I may be called to give him the special care I'm used to...
In the meantime, Engineer Serkö and Captain Spade are keeping a close eye on him.

Presumably, their intention is to let him be, and here’s what he does: After heading towards the main mast, which his eyes have vainly searched for sails, he reaches it, wraps his arms around it, and tries to shake it as if he wants to bring it down...
And then, seeing his fruitless efforts with the main mast, he attempts the same with the foremast.
His nervousness grows gradually.
Inarticulate cries follow the vague words that escape him...
Suddenly, he rushes towards the port shrouds and clings to them.
I wonder if he’s going to leap onto the stays, climbing up to the bars of the topgallant...
If he isn’t stopped, he risks falling onto the deck or, in a sudden roll, being thrown into the sea...

sentences: Oh!
oh!

I would prefer it locked with triple bolts!” Indeed, the small letter and the pin left by Andrea on the table confirmed, or rather supported, the sad truth.
Andrea had escaped.
We say supported, because the brigadier was not the kind of man to be convinced by a single piece of evidence.
He looked around him, peered under the bed, pulled back the curtains, opened the cupboards, and finally stopped at the fireplace.
Thanks to Andrea's precautions, no trace of his passage remained in the ashes.
However, it was an exit, and given the circumstances they were in, any exit warranted serious investigation.
The brigadier had a bundle of sticks and straw brought to him, stuffed the fireplace as he would have done with mortar, and set it on fire.
The fire made the brick walls crack; an opaque column of smoke shot up through the flues and rose to the sky like the dark jet of a volcano, but he did not see the prisoner fall, as he had expected.

This is because Andrea, from his youth fighting against society, was worth a gendarme, even if that gendarme had been promoted to the respectable rank of brigadier; anticipating the fire, he had made his way to the roof and was huddled against the pipe.

For a moment he had some hope of being saved, for he heard the brigadier calling the two gendarmes and shouting to them loudly: But as he stretched his neck out gently, he saw that the two gendarmes, instead of withdrawing, as would be natural, at the first announcement, he saw, let us say, that on the contrary, the two gendarmes were redoubling their attention.

sentences: It was on May 17th, about five hundred miles from Heart's Content, at a depth of two thousand eight hundred meters, that I spotted the cable lying on the sea floor.
Conseil, whom I hadn't warned, initially mistook it for a gigantic sea serpent and was preparing to classify it according to his usual method.
But I disabused the worthy fellow, and to console him for his disappointment, I taught him various details about the laying of this cable.
The operation went smoothly.
However, an incident occurred.
Several times, while unrolling the cable, the electricians noticed that nails had recently been driven into it with the intent of damaging its core.
Captain Anderson, his officers, and his engineers gathered, deliberated, and announced that if the culprit was caught on board, he would be thrown overboard without further judgment.
Since then, the criminal attempt has not been repeated.
I did not expect to find the electric cable in its original state, just as it was when it left the manufacturing workshops.
The long cable, covered in shell debris and bristling with foraminifera, was encrusted in a rocky coating that protected it from boring mollusks.

It lay quietly, sheltered from the movements of the sea, and under pressure favorable for the transmission of the electric spark that travels from America to Europe in thirty-two hundredths of a second.
The lifespan of this cable will undoubtedly be infinite, as it has been observed that the gutta-percha sheath improves with its time in seawater.
Was Captain Nemo going to surface to land on the British Isles?
No.
To my great surprise, he descended south and returned towards the European seas.
As I rounded Emerald Isle, I caught a glimpse of Cape Clear and the Fastnet lighthouse, which lights up the thousands of ships coming from Glasgow or Liverpool.

sentences: You never had any complaints about him?
asked the governor of the jailer in charge of bringing the abbé's provisions.
Never, governor, replied the jailer, never, absolutely never!
On the contrary: he used to entertain me a lot by telling me stories; one day when my wife was ill, he even gave me a recipe that cured her.
Ah!
ah!
said the doctor, I didn't know I was dealing with a colleague; I hope, governor, he added with a laugh, that you will treat him accordingly.
Yes, yes, rest assured, he will be decently buried in the newest sack we can find; are you satisfied?

Of course, but let's hurry, I can't stay in this room all day." New comings and goings were heard; a moment later, the sound of crumpled fabric reached Dantès's ears, the bed creaked on its springs, a heavy step like that of a man lifting a burden pressed down on the stone, then the bed creaked again under the weight being returned to it.

Impossible, replied the governor; the castle chaplain came to ask me yesterday for a leave to make a short trip of eight days to Hyères, I told him about all my prisoners during that time; the poor abbé should have just not rushed so much, and he would have had his requiem.
Bah!

Hyères said the doctor with the irreverence familiar to people in his profession, he is a man of the Church: God will take the situation into account, and will not give hell the wicked pleasure of sending him a priest.

sentences: And he counted fifteen thousand francs in gold and thirty thousand francs in banknotes on the table.
--Wait until I light the lamp, said the Carconte, it's getting dark, and we might make a mistake.
Indeed, night had fallen during this discussion, and with the night, the storm that had been threatening for half an hour.
Thunder could be heard rumbling in the distance; but neither the jeweler, nor Caderousse, nor the Carconte seemed to care, as they were all three possessed by the demon of greed.
I myself felt a strange fascination at the sight of all this gold and all these banknotes.
It seemed to me that I was dreaming, and, as often happens in a dream, I felt chained to my place.
Caderousse counted and recounted the gold and the banknotes, then he passed them to his wife, who counted and recounted them in turn.

Meanwhile, the jeweler was making the diamond sparkle under the lamp's rays, and the diamond was throwing flashes that made him forget those which, as precursors of the storm, were starting to ignite the windows.

The Carconte went to a cupboard and returned with an old leather wallet, from which they took out some greasy letters to replace them with the banknotes, and a bag that contained two or three six-livre coins, which probably made up the entire fortune of the miserable household.
--There, said Caderousse, although you may have raised about ten thousand francs for us, would you like to have dinner with us?
It's with good heart.
--Thank you, said the jeweler, it must be getting late, and I need to return to Beaucaire; my wife would be worried;” he pulled out his watch.
Morbleu!
he exclaimed, it's almost nine o'clock, I won't be in Beaucaire before midnight.
Goodbye, my little children; if by chance you hear from the abbés Busoni, think of me.

sentences: I reassured him as best I could, glad to have come that very evening and to witness the spectacle of this superstitious terror.
I told stories, and I managed to calm almost everyone down.
By the hearth, an old, nearly blind, mustachioed dog—one of those dogs that resemble people we know—was sleeping with his nose tucked into his paws.

Outside, the fierce storm battered the little house, and through a narrow window, a sort of peephole near the door, I suddenly saw a jumble of trees being tossed by the wind in the light of bright flashes of lightning.
Despite my efforts, I could tell that a deep terror gripped these people, and every time I stopped speaking, all ears listened intently.

Tired of witnessing these foolish fears, I was about to ask to go to bed when the old gamekeeper suddenly jumped from his chair, grabbed his gun again, and stammered in a bewildered voice: "There it is!"
There it is!
I can hear it!" The two women fell to their knees in their corners, hiding their faces, while the sons picked up their axes.

I was about to try to calm them again when the sleeping dog suddenly woke up and, lifting his head, stretching his neck, looking toward the fire with his almost extinguished eye, let out one of those mournful howls that make travelers shudder in the countryside at night.
All eyes turned to him; he remained still, standing on his legs as if haunted by a vision, and he began to howl at something invisible, unknown, and surely terrifying, as all his fur bristled.
The gamekeeper, pale, shouted: "He senses it!"
He senses it!
He was there when I killed him." And the distraught women both began to howl along with the dog.

sentences: Franz sincerely complimented Albert; he received them like a man who deserves them.
He had recognized, he said, by certain signs of inimitable elegance, that his beautiful unknown must belong to the highest aristocracy.
While receiving this confidence, Franz noticed that Albert seemed to have something to ask him, yet he hesitated to make that request.
He insisted, declaring in advance that he was ready to make any sacrifices within his power for Albert's happiness.
Albert took just enough time to be polite: then finally he confessed to Franz that he would do him a favor by leaving him the carriage all to himself for the next day.
Albert attributed the extreme kindness shown by the beautiful peasant girl in lifting her mask to the absence of his friend.
It is clear that Franz was not selfish enough to stop Albert in the midst of an adventure that promised to be both delightful for his curiosity and flattering for his self-esteem.

He knew his worthy friend's perfect indiscretion well enough to be sure that he would keep him updated on every detail of his good fortune; and since, for the past two or three years, he had been traveling all over Italy, he had never even had the chance to embark on such an intrigue for himself, so Franz was not displeased to learn how things unfolded in such cases.
He therefore promised Albert that he would content himself the next day with watching the spectacle from the windows of the Rospoli palace.
Indeed, the next day he saw Albert passing by again and again.
He had a huge bouquet that he had undoubtedly tasked with being the bearer of his love letter.
This probability became certainty when Franz saw the same bouquet, distinguished by a circle of white camellias, in the hands of a charming peasant girl dressed in pink satin.
So in the evening, it was no longer joy, it was delirium.
Albert had no doubt that the beautiful unknown would respond to him in the same way.
Franz anticipated his desires by telling him that all this noise was tiring him, and that he had decided to spend the next day reviewing his album and taking notes.

sentences: The soldiers immediately crossed their bayonets, believing that the prisoner was rushing towards the inspector with ill intentions.

Then, he gathered in his gaze all that the human heart can hold of gentleness and humility, and expressing himself with a kind of pious eloquence that astonished those present, he tried to touch the soul of his visitor.
The inspector listened to Dantès' speech until the end, then turning to the governor, he said in a low voice, "He will turn to devotion; he is already inclined to softer feelings.
See, fear is having its effect on him; he recoiled before the bayonets; now, a madman does not recoil before anything: I have made some very curious observations on this subject at Charenton."
--I ask what crime I have committed; I ask to be given judges; I ask for my trial to be conducted; I finally ask to be shot if I am guilty, but also to be set free if I am innocent.
--Yes, I believe it, I know nothing.

But that matters little; what should matter, not only to me, the unfortunate prisoner, but also to all the officials administering justice, and even to the king who governs us, is that an innocent person is not a victim of an infamous denunciation and does not die behind bars cursing his executioners.
--You are quite humble today, said the governor; you have not always been like this.
You spoke quite differently, my dear friend, on the day you wanted to assault your guard.
--That's true, sir, said Dantès, and I humbly apologize to that man who has always been good to me....
But, what do you want?
I was mad, I was furious.
No, sir, for captivity has bent, broken, and annihilated me....
I've been here for so long!
Seventeen months!
Dantès replied.
Ah!

Sir, you don't know what seventeen months in prison is like: seventeen years, seventeen centuries; especially for a man who, like me, was on the verge of happiness, for a man who, like me, was about to marry a beloved woman, for a man who saw an honorable career opening up before him, and who now lacks everything; who, from the middle of the most beautiful day, falls into the deepest night, who sees his career destroyed, who doesn't know if the one who loved him still loves him, who is unaware if his old father is dead or alive.
Seventeen months in prison, for a man used to the sea air, to the independence of a sailor, to space, to vastness, to infinity!
Sir, seventeen months in prison is more than all the crimes that the most odious names in human language could ever deserve.
So have pity on me, sir, and ask for me, not leniency, but severity; not a pardon, but a judgment; judges, sir, all I ask for are judges; one cannot refuse judges to an accused person.

sentences: I would add that this man was proud, that his firm and calm gaze seemed to reflect lofty thoughts, and that from this whole, from the homogeneity of expressions in the gestures of the body and face, according to the observation of physiognomists, resulted an undeniable frankness.
I felt "involuntarily" reassured in his presence, and I had high hopes for our meeting.
Whether this man was thirty-five or fifty years old, I couldn't say.

He was tall, with a broad forehead, a straight nose, a distinctly shaped mouth, magnificent teeth, and fine, elongated hands, eminently "psychic"—to use a term from chirology—meaning worthy of serving a noble and passionate soul.
This man certainly represented the most admirable type I had ever encountered.
A particular detail: his eyes, slightly spaced apart, could simultaneously take in nearly a quarter of the horizon.
I later verified that this ability was accompanied by a vision power even greater than that of Ned Land.

When this stranger focused on an object, the line of his eyebrows furrowed, his wide eyelids drew closer together to encircle the pupils of his eyes and thus narrow the extent of his field of vision, and he looked!
What a gaze!
How it magnified objects diminished by distance!
How it penetrated you to the soul!
How it pierced through those liquid layers, so opaque to our eyes, and how it read to the depths of the seas!...
The two strangers, wearing berets made of sea otter fur and sea boots made of seal skin, were dressed in a particular fabric that accentuated their waists and allowed for great freedom of movement.
The taller of the two, obviously the leader on board, examined us with extreme attention, without uttering a word.
Then, turning to his companion, he conversed with him in a language I could not recognize.
It was a sonorous, harmonious, flexible idiom, whose vowels seemed subject to very varied accentuation.
The other responded with a nod and added two or three perfectly incomprehensible words.
Then, with his gaze, he seemed to question me directly.
I replied, in good French, that I did not understand his language; but he did not seem to understand me, and the situation became quite awkward.

sentences: I was crossing the great dunes south of Ouargla.
It is one of the strangest countries in the world.
You know the smooth sand, the straight sand of the endless beaches of the Ocean.
Well!
Imagine the Ocean itself turned to sand in the midst of a hurricane; picture a silent storm of motionless waves in yellow dust.
These waves are as high as mountains, uneven, different, raised just like wild waves, but even larger, and streaked like watered silk.
On this furious, silent, and motionless sea, the scorching sun of the south pours down its relentless and direct flame.
One must climb these golden ash waves, descend, climb again, climb endlessly, without rest and without shade.
The horses are groaning, sinking to their knees, and sliding down the other side of the surprising hills.
We were two friends followed by eight spahis and four camels with their camel drivers.
We no longer spoke, overwhelmed by heat, fatigue, and parched with thirst like this burning desert.
Suddenly one of these men let out a sort of cry; everyone stopped; and we remained still, surprised by an inexplicable phenomenon known to travelers in these remote lands.

Somewhere near us, in an indeterminate direction, a drum was beating, the mysterious drum of the dunes; it beat distinctly, sometimes more vibrantly, sometimes weakened, stopping, then resuming its fantastic rolling.

The Arabs, terrified, looked at each other; and one said in his language, 'Death is upon us.' And suddenly my companion, my friend, almost my brother, fell from his horse, headfirst, struck down by sunstroke.

And for two hours, while I tried in vain to save him, this elusive drum continually filled my ears with its monotonous, intermittent, and incomprehensible sound; and I felt fear, true fear, hideous fear, creeping into my bones, in front of that beloved corpse, in this hole scorched by the sun between four mounds of sand, while the unknown echo threw at us, two hundred leagues from any French village, the rapid beating of the drum.
That day, I understood what it was to be afraid; I learned it even better another time...

sentences: The two men continued to play; from time to time, a stronger gust from the hurricane shook the door, made the walls tremble, and the two drinkers looked up as if someone were about to enter.
Then Mathurin took the liter and filled Jérémie's glass.
But suddenly, the clock hanging on the counter struck midnight.
Its hoarse chime sounded like a clash of pots and pans, and the strikes resonated for a long time, with a metallic sound.

Mathurin immediately got up, like a sailor whose shift is over: The other moved with more difficulty, steadied himself by leaning on the table; then he made his way to the door and opened it while his companion turned off the lamp.

When they were in the street, Mathurin locked up the shop; then he said: Jérémie took three steps, then swayed, stretched out his hands, found a wall that supported him upright, and started moving again, stumbling.

At times, a gust of wind, rushing into the narrow street, pushed him forward, made him run a few steps; then when the violence of the storm ceased, he stopped abruptly, having lost his prop, and began to wobble again on his drunken, unsteady legs.
He was instinctively heading towards his home, like birds returning to their nests.
Finally, he recognized his door and began to feel around for the lock to insert the key.
He couldn't find the hole and cursed under his breath.

Then he banged on it with his fists, calling for his wife to come help him: He was no longer moving, stunned with fear, bewildered, in a devilish terror, haunted by all the mysterious things of the darkness, and he waited a long time without daring to make a move.
But, as he saw that nothing was stirring anymore, a bit of reason returned to him, the muddled reasoning of a drunkard.
And he sat down, very quietly.
He waited a long time again, and finally gathering his courage, he spoke: Then, all of a sudden, a doubt crossed his clouded mind, an indecisive doubt, a vague suspicion.
He did not move; he remained there, sitting on the ground, in the dark, searching for his thoughts, clinging to incomplete and stumbling reflections like his feet.

sentences: Indeed, just at the moment of this debacle, the temperature had dropped several degrees.
A thick fog soon enveloped all these areas of the Arctic Ocean, but it was not an ordinary fog.
The ground was covered, at its surface, with a white crust, very distinct from the frost.
This was nothing more than a water vapor that freezes after it precipitates.

The very fine particles that made up this fog clung to the trees, shrubs, and the walls of the fort, to everything that jutted out, and soon formed a thick layer, adorned with prismatic or pyramidal fibers, the tips of which pointed into the wind.
Jasper Hobson then recognized this meteorological phenomenon, which whalers and winterers have often noted appearing in the spring in polar regions.

"This is not fog," he said to his companions, "it's a frost-rime, a frozen mist, a dense vapor that remains in a state of complete freezing." However, whether it was fog or frozen mist, the appearance of this meteor was nonetheless regrettable, as it occupied a height of at least a hundred feet above sea level, and so complete was its opacity that, placed three steps apart, two people could not see each other.
The winterers' disappointment was great.
It seemed that nature wanted to spare them no trouble.

It was at the moment when the thaw was occurring, when the drifting island was about to break free from the bonds that had chained it for so many months, and finally when its movements were to be monitored more closely, that this fog came to obstruct all observation!
And it was like this for four days!
The frost-rime did not dissipate until April 15.
In the morning, a violent southerly breeze tore it apart and annihilated it.
The sun was shining.
Lieutenant Hobson threw himself on his instruments.
He took readings, and the result of his calculations for the current coordinates of the island was this: Kalumah was right.
The island of Victoria, caught by the Bering current, was drifting south.
The winterers were finally getting closer to the more frequented areas of the Bering Sea.
They no longer had to fear being swept north.
It was now just a matter of monitoring the island's movement and estimating its speed, which, due to obstacles, was likely to be quite uneven.
This was what Jasper Hobson meticulously occupied himself with, taking readings of the sun and stars in turn.

The very next day, April 16, after observation, he calculated that if the speed remained uniform, the island of Victoria would reach the Arctic Circle around the beginning of May, from which it was separated by no more than four degrees of latitude.

sentences: Victoria Island was then floating in the largest part of the Bering Sea, six hundred miles from the first Aleutians and more than two hundred miles from the nearest coast to the east.
Its movement was still occurring at a relatively considerable speed.
However, assuming it did not suffer any decrease, it would still need at least three weeks to reach that southern barrier of the Bering Sea.

Could this island last until then, whose base was thinning each day under the action of the already tepid waters, and brought to an average temperature of fifty degrees Fahrenheit (10° centigrade above zero)?
above zero?
Could its ground open up at any moment?
Lieutenant Hobson was urging with all his might the construction of the raft, whose lower frame was already floating on the lagoon's waters.
Mac Nap wanted to give this device a great solidity, so that it could withstand for a long time, if necessary, the shocks of the sea.
Indeed, it was to be assumed that, if he did not encounter any whaling ship in the Bering area, he would drift to the Aleutian Islands, and a long stretch of sea remained to be crossed.
However, Victoria Island had not yet experienced any significant change in its general configuration.

Reconnaissances were being made daily, but the explorers ventured out only with extreme caution, as at any moment, a fracture of the ground or a fragmentation of the island could isolate them from the common center.
Those who departed in this way could always be feared to not be seen again.
The deep cut located at the approaches of Cape Michel, which the winter's cold had closed, had gradually reopened.
It now extended for a mile inland to the dried-up bed of the small river.
One could even fear that it would follow this bed, which, already dug, was thinning the ice crust even more.
In this case, the entire portion between Cape Michel and Barnett Port, limited to the west by the riverbed, would have disappeared.
that is to say, an enormous piece, covering several square miles.

At the foot of the hill, the count dismounted, and by a small circular path, eighteen inches wide, began to climb the mountain; upon reaching the summit, he found himself stopped by a hedge where green fruits had replaced the pink and white flowers.
Monte Cristo searched for the gate of the small enclosure, and soon found it.
It was a small wooden portcullis, rolling on wicker hinges and closing with a nail and a string.
In an instant, the count understood the mechanism and the gate opened.

The count then found himself in a small garden twenty feet long and twelve feet wide, bounded on one side by the part of the hedge in which was framed the ingenious machine we described as the gate, and on the other by the old tower covered in ivy, all sprinkled with wildflowers and stock.

One would not have said, seeing it so wrinkled and flowered like a grandmother who has just received holiday wishes from her grandchildren, that it could recount many terrible dramas, if it could join a voice to the threatening ears that an old proverb attributes to walls.

One walked through this garden along a sandy path of red sand, on which a border of large boxwood, several years old, bit with colors that would have delighted the eye of Delacroix, our modern Rubens.
